setup.art: The square of cloth folded corner to corner, with a pencil line along the fold and two strips marked: one along the threads and one along the fold.
setup.caption: 2. Fold the square corner to corner. The fold is the slant, called the bias. Cut one strip along the threads and one along the slant.

setup.art: A cloth strip with two pencil marks 20 centimetres apart, clipped to a hook with a carry bag clipped to the bottom.
setup.caption: 3. Draw two marks 20 centimetres apart. Clip the strip to a hook. Clip a carry bag to the bottom.

setup.art: A water bottle in the carry bag hanging from the cloth strip, with a ruler held beside it measuring the length between the two marks.
setup.caption: 4. Put the bottle in the bag. Measure the length between the marks.

setup.art: Two strips side by side, one hardly stretched and one stretched into a long thin shape, with measuring numbers beside them.
setup.caption: 5. Do the other strip. Compare how much each one stretched.

flow.do: Show your child the cloth, the bottle and the clips. Ask for a guess and a reason before anything is cut. Write the guess at the top of the table.
flow.say: We will cut two strips from one cloth. One strip runs along the threads. The other runs on the slant. Each carries the same bottle. Which will stretch more? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess first. Which strip will stretch more? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Why do you think one strip might stretch more than the other?
good: The threads are in the way on the slant.
They are the same cloth, so they will be the same.
The threads cross, so the slant might give.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Write your child's own words.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Tailor's Trick test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Pull one thread out near the edge of the cloth. The gap it leaves is a straight line along the threads. Cut along the gap. Do the same on another side to make a square about 40 centimetres each way.
flow.say: Look at the cloth. You can see threads in two directions. Pull out one thread. The gap shows the straight line of the threads.
flow.kid: Pull out one thread near the edge. The gap shows the way the threads run.
flow.parent: Use woven cloth, not a knitted T-shirt. Knitted cloth is made of loops and stretches both ways. If the cloth has a printed stripe or check, you can also follow that. Do not worry if the square is not perfect.
flow.context: In this step, you find the line of the threads and cut the cloth into a square.

flow.do: Fold the square corner to corner, so the fold crosses the cloth at a slant. Press the fold and draw a pencil line along it. Cut one strip 5 centimetres wide and 35 centimetres long along the threads. Cut a second strip of the same size along the fold line.
flow.say: Fold the cloth from corner to corner. That fold is the slant, which tailors call the bias. Cut one strip along the threads and one along the bias.
flow.kid: Fold the cloth corner to corner. That fold is the bias. Cut one strip each way.

check.q: Why are the two strips the same width and length?
options: So that they fit on the hook
So that only the direction of the cut is different
So that the strips look neat
check.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. If one strip were wider, you would not know if the width or the direction made the difference. Neatness and the hook are not the reasons.

flow.context: In this step, you cut a strip along the threads and a strip on the slant.

flow.do: Lay strip 1 flat and draw two pencil marks 20 centimetres apart. Clip the top of the strip to the hook. Clip a carry bag to the bottom. Measure between the marks. Then put the bottle in the bag, wait ten seconds, and measure again.
flow.say: Mark two points 20 centimetres apart. Hang the strip, with the bag clipped to the bottom. Measure. Then add the bottle. Wait ten seconds and measure again.
flow.kid: Mark 20 centimetres. Hang the strip. Add the bottle. Measure again.
flow.parent: Hold the bag steady while someone reads the ruler, because a swinging bag gives wrong numbers. Along the threads, the marks may stay almost 20 centimetres apart. On the slant they may stretch by 2 to 5 centimetres. A very old or loose cloth may stretch more. Read the ruler at eye level.
flow.context: In this step, you hang the first strip with the bottle and measure how much it stretches.

flow.do: Do the other strip in the same way. Then do each strip a second time. Write the stretch for each try. The stretch is the length with the bottle minus 20 centimetres.
flow.say: Now test the other strip in the same way. Then test both strips again. Subtract 20 from each hanging length to find the stretch.
flow.kid: Test the other strip. Then test both again. Work out the stretch.
flow.context: In this step, you test the second strip and repeat both tests.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened. Then look closely at the cloth and its threads in bright light.
flow.say: Write three sentences. What did you think? What did you see? Why do you think it happened? Then look closely at the threads.
flow.kid: Say or write three sentences. What I think. What I saw. Why it happened.

ask.q: What do you think the threads did on the slant?
good: They turned, so the squares became diamonds.
They did not stretch, but they moved.
They swung to a new angle.

flow.parent: A good reason says that threads hardly stretch. Along the threads, the pull goes straight into them. On the slant, the threads swing to a new angle, so the cloth gets longer without stretching its threads. Let your child try first. Then read the Cloth card together.
flow.context: In this step, you explain what you found and look at the weave.

experiments.title: Bend Until It Snaps: how many bends does a paper clip survive?
experiments.question: How many bends does it take to snap a paper clip? Does a big bend or a small bend snap it sooner?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. How many big bends will it take to snap a paper clip? Will small bends take more bends, or fewer? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: All the clips are the same kind, from the same box. You straighten each one in the same way and bend it at the middle. Three clips get big bends and three clips get small bends. You count every bend in the same way. Only the size of the bend changes.
results_table: Number of bends until it snapped

materials.item: 8 steel paper clips of the same kind, from one box
a corner cut from a notebook cover or a book, to show a right angle
a pencil and the results table
a magnifying glass, if you have one
a small bowl to catch the snapped pieces

experiments.safety: A grown-up stays close. The wire can spring and the snapped ends are sharp. Hold the wire low and away from your face, and wear glasses if you have them. Put the pieces in the bowl at once, then in the bin, and keep them away from children under five.
experiments.record: For each clip, write the size of bend and the number of bends before it snapped. Then find the average for the big bends and for the small bends.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you bend straightened paper clips back and forth until they snap. You count how many bends it takes, for big bends and for small bends.

setup.art: A paper clip being unfolded and straightened into a single piece of wire about 9 centimetres long.
setup.caption: 1. Unfold a paper clip into a straight wire.

setup.art: A notebook corner held beside a bent wire to show a big bend, a right angle, and half of that for a small bend.
setup.caption: 2. A big bend makes a right angle. A small bend makes half of a right angle.

setup.art: A child holding a wire low with two fingers and bending the end one way to the book corner, then back the other way.
setup.caption: 3. Bend the wire to one side, then to the other. Count every bend.

setup.art: A wire snapped in two over a small bowl, with the child touching the bent place with a finger.
setup.caption: 4. When it snaps, put the pieces in the bowl. Touch the place where it bent.

setup.art: A table with six clips and their bend counts written in two columns, big bends and small bends.
setup.caption: 5. Write the number of bends for each clip in the table.

flow.do: Show your child the paper clips and the bowl. Ask for a guess and a reason before bending anything. Write the guess at the top of the table.
flow.say: We will bend a paper clip back and forth until it snaps. How many bends will it take? Will small bends take more or fewer? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess first. How many bends will snap a paper clip? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Why do you think a clip might snap after only a few bends?
good: The metal gets tired.
Each bend hurts the metal a little.
It breaks when it cannot bend any more.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Write your child's own words.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Bend Until It Snaps test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Unfold 8 paper clips into straight wires. Show your child the corner of the notebook. Say that this is a right angle. A big bend makes a right angle. A small bend makes half of it.
flow.say: Straighten each clip into a wire. A big bend turns the wire to a right angle. A small bend turns it only half as far.
flow.kid: Straighten the clips. A big bend is a right angle. A small bend is half of that.
flow.parent: Each clip is straightened in the same way. Keep two for spares. Mark the three for big bends with B and the three for small bends with S on the results table.
flow.context: In this step, you straighten the clips and learn the two sizes of bend.

flow.do: Hold a wire low, with about 2 centimetres sticking out from your fingers. Bend the end to one side until it makes a right angle. That is bend 1. Bend it to the other side. That is bend 2. Keep counting until it snaps. Do this with three wires.
flow.say: Hold the wire low. Bend the end to one side. Count one. Bend it the other way. Count two. Keep going until it snaps.
flow.kid: Bend the wire to one side. Count one. Bend it back. Count two. Keep going.
flow.parent: Big bends usually snap a clip in fewer than 15 bends. Clips vary, so write down what you get. Do not worry if one clip takes far more or far fewer bends than the others.
flow.context: In this step, you test three wires with big bends and count the bends until each snaps.

flow.do: Now take three more wires. Bend them only half as far, to half a right angle. Count every bend. Stop if you reach 60 bends, and write 60 or more. Put each snapped piece in the bowl.
flow.say: Do the same with three new wires, but bend them only half as far. Count every bend. Stop at 60.
flow.kid: Bend three new wires half as far. Count every bend. Stop at 60.
flow.parent: Small bends usually take longer. Many clips need between 15 and 50 bends, and some do not break in 60. Stop at 60 and write 60 or more. A common sign of a good test is that the bigger bends snap the clip sooner.

check.q: Why do we use the same size of bend for all three wires in a group?
options: So that the wires stay clean
So that all the wires snap at once
So that only one thing changes between the two groups
check.why: In a fair test, you change one thing and keep the rest the same. If the bends were different sizes within a group, you could not say that the size of the bend caused the difference. Snapping at once or staying clean has no link to the test.

flow.context: In this step, you test three wires with small bends and count the bends until each snaps.

flow.do: Take one snapped clip. Touch the place where it bent. Is it warm? Look at the two broken ends with a magnifying glass. Ask your child where the heat might have come from.
flow.say: Touch the place where the wire bent. Is it warm? Look at the broken ends. What do they look like?
flow.kid: Touch the bent place. Is it warm? Look at the broken ends.

ask.q: Where do you think the warmth came from?
good: From bending. Bending is work, and work makes heat.
From my fingers.
From rubbing inside the metal.

flow.parent: The bent place can feel warm after many bends. The work done by your hand turns into a little heat. The broken ends often look bright and grainy, because a fresh break shows the metal's inside. The snapped ends are sharp, so keep them in the bowl.
flow.context: In this step, you feel the bent place and look at the break.

flow.do: Find the average for the big bends and for the small bends. Add the three numbers and divide by 3. Draw a bar for each group. Then ask your child to say or write three sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Find the average number of bends for each group. Then write three sentences. What did you think? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Find the average for each group. Say or write three sentences.
flow.parent: A good reason says that each bend does a little damage to the inside of the metal. Tiny cracks start and grow. Bigger bends do more damage each time. Let your child try first. Then read the Fatigue card together.
flow.context: In this step, you work out the averages and explain what you found.

activities.title: Grain Hunt: split, tear and snap

materials.item: 2 thin bamboo skewers with blunt ends
2 wooden ice-cream sticks
1 celery stalk
1 banana leaf, or another long leaf with parallel veins, such as a coconut leaflet
a magnifying glass, if you have one
a sheet of paper, a pencil and a tray

activities.safety: Use the blunt ends of the skewers and keep the sharp points on the tray. Do not put sticks near your face, and watch for splinters when wood snaps. A grown-up checks that nobody is allergic to celery, and the celery is not for eating. Wash your hands after touching the leaf and the celery.

schedule.what: Guess where each thing splits. Test each one. Draw the grain arrows. Sort the things.

activities.record: A table with each thing, your guess, what happened and an arrow drawn along its grain.
activities.context: In this activity, you try to split, tear and snap six things in two directions. You find which direction gives way more easily, and draw the grain.

setup.art: Six things lined up on a tray: two bamboo skewers, two ice-cream sticks, a celery stalk and a banana leaf, each with a pencil arrow beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Line up the things. Guess how each one will split.

setup.art: A child's thumbnail pushing down the blunt end of a bamboo skewer to start a split along its length.
setup.caption: 2. Try to split each stick along its length with a thumbnail.

setup.art: A banana leaf being torn from the edge towards the middle, with the straight tear following the veins.
setup.caption: 3. Tear the leaf from the edge, then try along the middle.

setup.art: A magnifying glass held over the torn edge of a leaf and over a split stick, showing long fibres.
setup.caption: 4. Look at each torn edge. Draw an arrow along the grain.

flow.do: Line up the six things on the tray. Ask your child to guess for each one whether it will split more easily along its length or across it. Write the guesses.
flow.say: Look at each thing. Where do you think it will split most easily? Along its length, or across? Write your guess for each one.
flow.kid: Look at the six things. Guess how each one will split. Write it down.

ask.q: Which thing do you think will be hardest to guess?
good: The celery.
The ice-cream stick.
The leaf.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guesses. Any guess is fine.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Grain Hunt. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Hold a skewer by its blunt end. Push your thumbnail into the end and try to split it down its length. Then bend the skewer until it snaps across. Do the same with an ice-cream stick.
flow.say: Press your thumbnail into the end of the stick. Does it split along its length? Now bend it to snap it across. Which was easier?
flow.kid: Split the stick along its length. Then snap it across. Which was easier?
flow.parent: A thin bamboo skewer often splits when you push a thumbnail into its blunt end. A flat ice-cream stick may need more force. If it does not split, press harder or ask a grown-up to start the split. Either way, write down what happens. Wood and bamboo split along the grain much more easily than across.
flow.context: In this step, you split and snap a bamboo skewer and an ice-cream stick.

flow.do: Take the celery stalk. Snap the end and pull gently so a string peels off. Then take the banana leaf. Tear it from the edge towards the middle. Then try tearing it lengthwise along the middle.
flow.say: Snap the end of the celery and pull. Do strings peel off? Tear the leaf from the edge. Then try along the middle.
flow.kid: Peel a string off the celery. Tear the leaf from the edge. Then tear it along the middle.

check.q: The banana leaf tore easily from the edge inwards, but not lengthwise. What does that show?
options: The leaf is the same in every direction
The leaf is old and weak
The veins run in lines, and the leaf splits between them
check.why: A leaf with parallel veins splits between them, where only the thin leaf tissue holds the sides together. It is not old or weak. If the leaf were the same in every direction, it would tear the same way each time.

flow.context: In this step, you test the celery and the banana leaf.

flow.do: Look at each torn or split edge with the magnifying glass. Draw each thing on your paper. Draw an arrow along its grain.
flow.say: Look at the torn edges. What do you see? Draw each thing. Draw an arrow along the grain.
flow.kid: Look at the edges. Draw each thing. Draw its grain arrow.
flow.context: In this step, you look closely at the edges and draw the grain arrows.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Write three sentences. What did you think? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three sentences. What I think. What I saw. Why it happened.
flow.parent: A good reason says that these materials are built of long fibres or veins lying in lines. A split slips between the lines, and a snap has to break through them.
flow.context: In this step, you explain what you found.

activities.title: The Cardboard Bridge: flutes along or flutes across?

materials.item: 1 corrugated cardboard box, cut flat by a grown-up
scissors, used by a grown-up
a ruler and a pencil
2 stacks of books with a 20 centimetre gap between them
a 500 millilitre bottle of water, with its cap on tight
a sheet of paper and the results table

activities.safety: A grown-up does the cutting. Keep the bottle away from the edge of the table, and keep your feet away from the books in case they fall.

schedule.what: Find the flutes. Cut two strips. Test each strip as a bridge. Compare.

activities.record: A table with two strips, the direction of the flutes, the sag with the bottle and a drawing of each bridge.
activities.context: In this activity, you cut two strips from a corrugated cardboard box. One has the flutes along its length and the other has them across. You test which makes a stronger bridge.

setup.art: The cut edge of a corrugated cardboard sheet, showing a wavy middle layer between two flat layers, with an arrow along the waves.
setup.caption: 1. Look at the cut edge. The waves are the flutes. Draw an arrow along them.

setup.art: Two cardboard strips side by side, one with flutes running along its length and one with flutes across, each 6 centimetres wide and 25 centimetres long.
setup.caption: 2. Cut two strips. One has the flutes along its length. The other has them across.

setup.art: A cardboard strip bridging a gap of 20 centimetres between two stacks of books, with a water bottle lying across the middle.
setup.caption: 3. Lay the strip across the gap. Put the bottle in the middle.

setup.art: A ruler held beside a bridge to measure how far the middle has sagged below the books.
setup.caption: 4. Measure how far the middle sags.

flow.do: Show your child the flat cardboard and the bottle. Ask which strip will make the stronger bridge, and why. Write the guess.
flow.say: We will cut two strips from a cardboard box. One runs along the waves inside. The other runs across the waves. Which will carry the bottle better? Why?
flow.kid: Guess first. Which strip makes the stronger bridge? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Why do you think one strip might be stronger than the other?
good: The waves might work like little arches.
Both strips are the same cardboard.
The waves might make it stiffer one way.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Cardboard Bridge. You guess before you test.

flow.do: A grown-up looks at the cut edge of the box for the waves inside. These are the flutes. Draw an arrow along them. Cut a strip 6 centimetres wide and 25 centimetres long with the flutes along its length. Cut another with the flutes across its length.
flow.say: Look at the cut edge. See the waves between the flat layers? Draw an arrow along them. Now cut the two strips.
flow.kid: Find the waves on the cut edge. Draw an arrow. A grown-up cuts two strips.
flow.parent: Cut both strips to the same size. The strips need to be 25 centimetres long so that they rest well on the books. Write 'flutes along' on one and 'flutes across' on the other.
flow.context: In this step, you find the flutes and cut two strips.

flow.do: Set the two stacks of books 20 centimetres apart. Lay the strip with the flutes along its length across the gap. Lay the bottle across the middle. Measure how far the middle sags. Do the same with the other strip.
flow.say: Lay each strip across the gap. Put the bottle in the middle. Measure how far the strip sags. Write down both numbers.
flow.kid: Lay a strip across the gap. Put the bottle on. Measure the sag.
flow.parent: The strip with flutes along its length is usually very stiff and sags hardly at all. The strip with flutes across may sag by several centimetres or fold flat. If it folds, write 'folded'. Do not worry if the difference is smaller than you expected, as boxes vary.

check.q: The strip with the flutes along its length sagged much less. Why?
options: The bottle weighs less on that strip
The strip with flutes along is thicker
The flutes work like a row of little arches along the strip
check.why: The flutes make the cardboard stiff along their length, because the waves hold the two flat layers apart. The two strips came from the same box and have the same thickness. The bottle weighs the same on both.

flow.context: In this step, you test both strips as bridges and measure the sag.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened. Then look at the cut edge again and draw it with its waves.
flow.say: Write three sentences. What did you think? What did you see? Why do you think it happened? Then draw the cut edge.
flow.kid: Say or write three sentences. What I think. What I saw. Why it happened.
flow.parent: A good reason says that the waves hold the two flat layers apart, like a row of arches. Along the waves, they work as a beam. Across them, they fold like a concertina.
flow.context: In this step, you explain what you found and draw the cut edge.

activities.title: Paper Bridges: flat, folded or rolled?

materials.item: 4 sheets of A4 printer paper, all the same
transparent tape
2 stacks of books with a 15 centimetre gap between them
60 identical coins, such as one-rupee coins, or 60 identical small items such as steel washers
a small plastic cup to hold the coins
a sheet of paper and the results table

activities.safety: Keep coins away from children under five, who might put them in their mouths.

schedule.what: Make four bridges from four identical sheets. Load each with coins. Compare.

activities.record: A table with four bridges, their shape and the number of coins each one carried. Draw each bridge from the side.
activities.context: In this activity, you make four bridges from identical sheets of paper in four shapes. You find which shape carries the most coins.

setup.art: Four paper bridges side by side: a flat sheet, a zigzag-folded sheet, a rolled tube and a sheet with its edges folded up like a tray.
setup.caption: 1. Make four bridges: flat, zigzag, tube and tray.

setup.art: A flat sheet of paper across a 15 centimetre gap, sagging under a cup with a few coins.
setup.caption: 2. Lay the flat sheet across the gap. Put the cup in the middle. Add coins.

setup.art: A zigzag-folded paper bridge across the gap holding a cup full of coins.
setup.caption: 3. Test the folded bridge in the same way. Add coins until it sags.

setup.art: A table with four bridges in a row and a coin count written under each.
setup.caption: 4. Write the coin count for each bridge.

flow.do: Show your child the four sheets. Say that all four are the same paper. Ask which shape will carry the most coins, and which will carry the fewest. Write the guess.
flow.say: We have four sheets of paper, all the same. We fold them into four shapes. Which bridge will carry the most coins? Which the fewest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess first. Which shape carries the most coins? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Why do you think that shape will be the strongest?
good: It is thicker.
It has folds that hold it up.
A tube is strong.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This is the first step of Paper Bridges. You guess before you build.

flow.do: Make the four bridges. Leave the first sheet flat. Fold the second into a zigzag with six folds each about 2 centimetres wide. Roll the third into a tube and tape the seam. Fold the edges of the fourth up by 2 centimetres on the two long sides, so it looks like a tray.
flow.say: Leave one sheet flat. Fold one into a zigzag. Roll one into a tube and tape it. Fold the edges of one up, like a tray.
flow.kid: Make four bridges. Flat. Zigzag. Tube. Tray.
flow.parent: Keep the long edge of the paper as the span, so the folds run along the bridge. Use the same amount of tape on every bridge, or none if the shape stays. Make sure each bridge rests 2 centimetres on each stack of books.
flow.context: In this step, you build the four bridges from the same paper.

flow.do: Lay the flat sheet across the gap. Put the cup in the middle. Add coins one at a time, gently. Stop when the middle touches the table or the bridge slips. Count the coins. Test the other three in the same way.
flow.say: Lay each bridge across the gap. Put the cup in the middle. Add coins one at a time. Count them. Stop when the bridge sags to the table.
flow.kid: Test each bridge. Add coins one at a time. Count them.
flow.parent: A flat sheet usually carries hardly any coins. A tube or zigzag can carry 20 or more. If a bridge twists, add coins more gently. Write the number you reach, even if it surprises you.

check.q: The zigzag bridge carried far more coins than the flat sheet. The paper was the same. What changed?
options: The kind of paper
The shape, which put some of the paper far from the middle
The amount of paper
check.why: All four sheets were the same paper and the same size. The folded shape makes the sheet stiffer, because paper far from the middle does most of the work in a bend. The amount and kind of paper did not change.

flow.context: In this step, you load each bridge with coins and count how many it carries.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Write three sentences. What did you think? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three sentences. What I think. What I saw. Why it happened.
flow.parent: A good reason says that the material is the same, but the shape is different. A property of a material, such as how stiff paper is, does not change. A property of an object, such as how stiff the bridge is, depends on its shape.
flow.context: In this step, you explain what you found.

activities.title: Plywood Edge Detective: find the crossed layers

materials.item: a plywood item with a cut edge you can see, such as the edge of a shelf, a cupboard door or a drawer bottom
a magnifying glass, if you have one
a plank or a solid wooden stick, to compare
a sheet of paper and coloured pencils

schedule.what: Look at the edge of a plywood item. Count the layers. Draw the grain of each layer.

activities.record: A drawing of the plywood edge, with the layers counted and the grain direction of each one marked.
activities.context: In this activity, you look closely at the edge of a piece of plywood. You find the layers, and see how their grains are turned across each other.

setup.art: The cut edge of a plywood board showing five thin layers with lines of different directions, and a magnifying glass above it.
setup.caption: 1. Look closely at the edge of a plywood shelf or door.

setup.art: A drawing of a plywood edge with five layers, and a short arrow drawn on each layer showing which way its grain runs.
setup.caption: 2. Count the layers. Draw an arrow for the grain on each one.

flow.do: Find an item made of plywood. Look at its cut edge. Ask your child what they notice. Do not explain yet.
flow.say: Look at the edge of this board. What do you notice? What do you wonder?
flow.kid: Look at the edge of the board. What do you notice?

ask.q: What do you notice about the edge?
good: There are thin stripes.
It is made of layers.
Some lines go one way and some another.

flow.parent: Plywood furniture is common: look at the back of a cupboard, a drawer bottom, a bed base or a school desk. The layers are thin and look like stripes. Let your child count them.
flow.context: This is the first step of Plywood Edge Detective. You look before you learn.

flow.do: Count the layers. Use the magnifying glass if you have one. Look at the surface of each layer if you can see it. Draw the edge and an arrow for the grain on each layer.
flow.say: Count the layers. Draw the edge, layer by layer. Draw an arrow for each grain direction.
flow.kid: Count the layers. Draw each one. Add its grain arrow.

check.q: A plywood board has five layers. Why do most plywood boards have an odd number of layers?
options: So that it is cheaper
So that the board is balanced and does not curl
Because odd numbers are stronger
check.why: With an odd number of layers, the layers on the two faces have their grain the same way, so the board is balanced and stays flat. The cost and the idea that odd numbers are stronger are not the reasons.

flow.context: In this step, you count the layers and draw their grain directions.

flow.do: Compare the plywood edge with the end of a plank. Ask your child to say or write three sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Look at the end of a plank, then at the plywood edge. Write three sentences. What did you think? What did you see? Why?
flow.kid: Compare the plank end with the plywood edge. Say or write three sentences.
flow.parent: A good reason says that each layer is turned across the one below. Where one layer is weak, the next is strong. So the board is much less likely to split along one line than a plank. The crossed layers also stop the board from shrinking or swelling too much.
flow.context: In this step, you compare plywood with solid wood.

projects.title: Paper Plywood: three layers, crossed or not?

materials.item: 6 sheets of newspaper from the same newspaper
white glue, such as Fevicol, about 4 tablespoons, mixed with an equal amount of water
an old brush or a folded rag to spread the glue
2 sheets of plastic, such as polythene bags cut open, to protect the books
3 or 4 heavy books
scissors, used by a grown-up
a ruler and a pencil
a heavy book and a table edge for the droop test

projects.safety: A grown-up cuts the paper. Wash your hands with water after using the glue, and keep glue away from your eyes and mouth.

schedule.what: Find the grain of the newspaper. Cut the pieces. Glue two boards and press them under books overnight.
Cut strips from each board and test them as in the droop test. Compare.

projects.record: A table with two boards, the droop of a strip cut each way from each board, and a sentence about what you found.
projects.context: In this project, you make two small boards from layers of newspaper. In one board all the layers have the grain the same way. In the other, the layers are crossed. You test which board is more even.

setup.art: Six rectangles of newspaper, each with a pencil arrow along the long side, and three of them turned with the arrow across.
setup.caption: 1. Cut the newspaper. Mark the grain arrow on every piece.

setup.art: Three newspaper layers being glued together with a brush, with the arrows all pointing the same way.
setup.caption: 2. Make board A: three layers with the grain the same way.

setup.art: Three newspaper layers being glued together, with the middle layer turned so its arrow points across the others.
setup.caption: 3. Make board B: three layers with the middle layer turned across.

setup.art: Two glued boards pressed flat under heavy books overnight, with plastic sheets above and below.
setup.caption: 4. Press both boards flat under books. Leave them overnight.

setup.art: Strips cut from the two boards and tested as in the droop test, one along and one across each board.
setup.caption: 5. Next day, cut strips from each board and test their droop.

flow.do: Show your child the newspaper and the glue. Ask which board will be more even in every direction, and why. Write the guess.
flow.say: We will make two boards from three layers of newspaper each. In one, the layers all lie the same way. In the other, the middle one is turned across. Which board will be more even? Why?
flow.kid: Guess first. Which board will be more even? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Why might turning one layer across make the board more even?
good: The turned layer is strong where the others are weak.
It has more glue.
The layers cross.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This is the first step of Paper Plywood. You guess before you build.

flow.do: Tear a corner of each newspaper sheet down and across to find the straight tear. Draw an arrow along it. A grown-up cuts six rectangles, each 15 centimetres by 25 centimetres. Cut five with the arrow along the long side. Cut one with the arrow along the short side.
flow.say: Find the straight tear on each sheet. Draw an arrow. Then a grown-up cuts six pieces. Five with the arrow along the long side. One with it across.
flow.kid: Find the grain on each sheet. Draw an arrow. A grown-up cuts six pieces.
flow.parent: You can use the same rule as in the tear test. Keep the arrows visible on every piece. Board A uses three pieces with the arrow along the long side. Board B uses two of those, and the piece with the arrow along the short side goes in the middle.
flow.context: In this step, you find the grain and cut six pieces of newspaper.

flow.do: Mix the glue with an equal amount of water. For board A, brush glue on one piece. Lay a second piece on it with the arrow the same way. Brush it, and add the third. For board B, do the same but make the middle piece the one with the arrow across. Smooth out the bubbles with your hand.
flow.say: Brush glue on the first piece. Lay the second on top. Brush it. Lay the third on top. For board B, turn the middle piece across.
flow.kid: Glue three layers into board A. Glue board B with the middle layer turned.
flow.parent: Use thin glue so the paper does not tear. Smooth the layers from the middle outwards to push out bubbles. Do not drench the paper, or the boards will wrinkle.

check.q: In board B, why do we turn the middle layer across the other two?
options: So that the weak direction of one layer is covered by the strong direction of another
So that the glue goes further
So that the board is thicker
check.why: A layer is weaker across its grain. If the middle layer is turned, its strong direction lies across the weak direction of the other two. The amount of glue and the thickness do not change when you turn a layer.

flow.context: In this step, you glue the two boards.

flow.do: Lay each board between two sheets of plastic. Put them under the heavy books. Leave them overnight.
flow.say: Put each board between plastic sheets. Stack the heavy books on top. Leave them to dry until tomorrow.
flow.kid: Press the boards under heavy books. Leave them overnight.
flow.parent: Boards that dry without weight will curl. Board A may curl more than board B. Write down if you see this.
flow.wait: Leave the boards under the books overnight
flow.context: In this step, you press the boards flat while they dry.

flow.do: Take out the boards. A grown-up cuts a strip 3 centimetres wide from each board along the long side, and another across the short side. Put each strip on the table with 6 centimetres sticking out and the book on the end. Measure the droop. Do each strip twice. Write the numbers.
flow.say: Cut one strip from each board along the long side and one across. Test each strip's droop. Write down the numbers. Which board is more even?
flow.kid: Cut strips from both boards. Test their droop. Compare along and across.

ask.q: What do you notice about the two boards?
good: Board A drooped more one way than the other.
Board B was more even.
The crossed board was stiffer.

flow.parent: Board A should droop less when cut along the grain than across. Board B should droop about the same either way. Papers vary, so the difference may be small. Write what you see. A good reason says the crossed layer evens out the direction. Read the Crossed Layers card together.
flow.context: On day two, you test the boards. You find which board is more even.

challenges.title: The Paper Beam: carry the most with two sheets
challenges.problem: You have two sheets of A4 printer paper and a little tape. Build a beam that spans a gap of 20 centimetres between two stacks of books, and carries as many coins as possible in a cup at its middle.
constraints: Use only two sheets of A4 paper and up to 40 centimetres of tape.
The beam must rest on the two stacks of books, 20 centimetres apart, with 2 centimetres on each stack.
The coins must go in a cup in the middle, and be added one at a time.
The beam must hold for ten seconds with the coins on it.
general: A paper tube rolled along the span and taped, so the paper wall is round.
A zigzag-folded sheet laid across the gap, like the folded bridge in Paper Bridges.
A tray shape with the edges folded up, to stiffen it along its length.
creative: A triangular tube, which is stiffer than a round one because its corners hold its shape.
A tube with rings of tape around it at intervals, like the nodes of bamboo, to stop the walls from folding in.
Two thin tubes side by side, joined by a flat top, like an I-beam, with the grain of the paper along the span.
challenges.your_turn: Sketch your design. Find the grain of the paper with a tear test, and decide which way to put it. Build your beam and test it. Change one thing, such as the shape or the way the grain runs, and test again. Which design carried the most coins? Why do you think it did?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about how shape and grain make paper stiffer. You build the strongest beam you can from two sheets of paper.

setup.art: A child sketching three beam designs on paper: a tube, a zigzag and a triangular tube, with arrows showing the grain.
setup.caption: 1. Sketch some designs and decide which way the grain runs.

setup.art: A paper tube bridging a 20 centimetre gap between two stacks of books, with a cup of coins on its middle.
setup.caption: 2. Build your beam. Rest it on the books with the cup in the middle.

setup.art: A table showing three paper beams in different shapes, each with a coin count written beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Test and compare. Write the number of coins each beam carries.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Ask your child to tear a corner of the paper to find the grain. Then ask them to sketch two or three different beam designs, and mark the grain direction on each.
flow.say: You have two sheets of paper and a little tape. How could you shape them to carry the most? Find the grain first. Then draw some ideas.
flow.kid: Find the grain of the paper. Draw some beam ideas.

ask.q: What would make a paper beam carry more?
good: A tube shape.
Folds that run along the beam.
The grain running along the beam.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Paper Beam challenge. You plan before you build.

flow.do: Build your first design. Rest it on the books with the cup in the middle. Add coins one at a time. Count them. Keep going until it sags to the table or twists away. Write down the number.
flow.say: Build your first beam. Put the cup in the middle. Add coins one at a time. Count them. Write the number down, so you have something to beat.
flow.kid: Build your beam. Add coins one at a time. Count them. Write the number.
flow.parent: Place the cup carefully in the middle. Add coins gently so the beam does not twist. The first number is the one to beat.
flow.context: In this step, you build your first design and test it.

flow.do: Change one thing, such as the shape, the way the grain runs or where the tape goes. Build the new beam and test it in the same way. Write down the number. Try a third design if you have time.
flow.say: Change just one thing about the beam. Build it again. Test it. Did it carry more or fewer coins?
flow.kid: Change one thing. Build again. Test it. Write the number.
flow.parent: Common changes are turning the grain to run along the span, making the tube thinner, or adding a fold along the middle. If a design twists, add tape rings.

check.q: Why do you change only one thing between your first and second beam?
options: So you know what made the difference
So you use less paper
So the second beam is easier to build
check.why: If you change two things, you cannot tell which one made the beam carry more or fewer coins. Changing one thing at a time is how you learn what works.

flow.context: In this step, you change one thing and test a second design.

flow.do: Compare your designs. Read the usual solutions and the creative ideas together. Ask your child to say which design was best and why. Invent a new one if you have time.
flow.say: Which beam carried the most? Why do you think so? Read the other ideas. Could you invent a new one?
flow.kid: Which beam carried the most? Why? Read the other ideas.

ask.q: What made your best beam stiff?
good: The shape put paper far from the middle.
The grain ran along it.
The tape rings stopped it folding in.

flow.context: In this step, you compare your designs and think about others.

quiz.p: Which sentence best describes a material that has a grain?
opts: It behaves differently when pulled in different directions
It is always made of wood
quiz.why: A grain is a direction in the material, set by fibres, cells, threads or layers lying in lines. Colour and kind of material do not decide it. Picking 'weak' mixes up direction with strength.

quiz.p: How could you find out which way the fibres lie in a sheet of newspaper?
opts: Hold it up to the light
Tear it in two directions and see which tear is straighter
quiz.why: A tear runs most easily between the lines of fibres, so the straighter tear shows the grain. Weight, light and smell do not show a direction.

quiz.p: Why does a bamboo stick split so easily along its length?
opts: Its strong fibres run along it, and little holds the sides together
quiz.why: Bamboo is packed with fibres lying along the stem. A split follows the gaps between them. A force across the fibres has to break them. Picking 'soft all through' misses that the direction matters.

quiz.p: Two bridges are made from identical sheets of paper. One is flat and sags under a coin. The other is rolled into a tube and carries many coins. What is the best explanation?
opts: Coins weigh less on a tube
The tube is made of a stronger paper
The shape of the tube is stiffer, though the paper is the same
quiz.why: The paper is the same. Rolling it puts the paper far from the middle, where it does the most work against a bend. A property of the object, its stiffness, changed. The property of the material did not.

quiz.p: Why is plywood less likely to split along one line than a plank?
opts: The layers cross, so each covers the weak direction of the next
It is made of harder wood
quiz.why: Each layer of plywood has its grain turned across the one below. Where one layer would split, the next holds. Glue holds the layers together, but it is not the reason for the evenness.

quiz.p: A glass tumbler is stiff, yet a small knock can shatter it. Which word describes glass best?
quiz.why: Glass takes in very little energy before it breaks, so it is not tough. It does not bend much first, so it is brittle. Stiff, tough and strong are different properties.

quiz.p: A paper clip bent once does not break, but after about ten bends it snaps. What is this called?
quiz.why: Fatigue is damage that builds up when a material is loaded again and again. Each bend lengthens tiny cracks, until the wire cannot hold.

quiz.p: A strip of woven cloth cut on the slant stretched 4 centimetres under a bottle. A strip cut along the threads stretched only 0.2 centimetres. What can you say?
opts: Woven cloth stretches far more on the slant than along its threads
quiz.why: The strips came from one cloth and carried the same bottle. The only difference was the direction of the cut. So the difference in stretch comes from the direction.
True. Glass has no lines of fibres or layers, so it is almost the same in every direction. Wood, paper and woven cloth are not.

quiz.p: What can designers already do with the inside of a material?
opts: Make a material that has no atoms
Choose any property they like with no testing
Arrange layers, fibres and holes so that the material does something new
Make a material that is the same as any other
quiz.why: Designers can build the inside, for example with layers in plywood or hinged shapes in an auxetic foam. They cannot yet choose any property they like, and every new design needs testing.

quiz.p: Which question can scientists still not answer reliably?
opts: Exactly how long a particular steel part will last, worked out from its atoms alone
Which way a banana leaf tears
quiz.why: Real materials have cracks, mixed ingredients and crystal edges that are hard to calculate, so tests on real samples are still needed. The other questions have clear answers.

quiz.p: A strip of a material is stiffer along its grain than across it. This means the material is ____, which means different in different directions.
quiz.why: Anisotropic comes from Greek words meaning not equal in all ways. Wood, paper and woven cloth are anisotropic.

applications: Building boats, furniture and roofs with wood cut so that the grain runs the strongest way.
Making plywood and laminated timber for doors, floors, boat hulls and school desks.
Weaving, stitching and cutting cloth, such as cutting on the bias for a neckline or a drape.

open_questions.q: How does a living tree decide which way to lay down new fibres as she grows?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know that trees sense bending and lean, and build special wood in answer. How a cell senses a push and chooses where to put new fibres is still being studied.

open_questions.q: Can we ever predict all the properties of a material from its atoms alone?
open_questions.why_open: For simple crystals, computers can calculate some properties well. For real materials, with cracks, mixtures and crystal edges, the calculation is too hard, and scientists disagree about how close we are.

open_questions.q: How can we tell, before it happens, exactly when a metal part will fail by fatigue?
open_questions.why_open: Engineers have good rules for how many bends a part can take on average. Predicting when one particular part will crack is still uncertain, because tiny flaws vary from part to part.

open_questions.q: Is there a limit to how strong a material can be?
open_questions.why_open: Calculations give a very high limit for a perfect crystal, and real materials are far weaker because of flaws. Whether we can make large pieces that come close to the limit is not known.

open_questions.q: Can a material be built so that it heals its own cracks?
open_questions.why_open: Living things heal their wounds, and bone repairs a break. Scientists have made small samples of plastics and concrete that heal tiny cracks, but making this work in large, everyday parts is still an open problem.

open_questions.q: How did the first people learn to split wood and bamboo along the grain?
open_questions.why_open: No written records survive from that time. We know that stone tools, wedges and split bamboo are very old, but not who first used the grain on purpose.

maths.problem: In the droop test, strip A drooped 3 centimetres and strip X drooped 6 centimetres. How many times as far did strip X droop as strip A?
maths.explain: Strip X drooped 6 centimetres and strip A drooped 3 centimetres. 6 divided by 3 is 2. So strip X, cut across the grain, drooped twice as far.
maths.context: In the droop test, you cut one strip along the grain and one across it, and measure how far each tip drops.
maths.why_maths: Dividing one result by the other tells you how many times bigger the difference is, which is easier to compare than two separate numbers.

maths.problem: A plank is doubled in thickness and becomes about 8 times as stiff, because 2 times 2 times 2 is 8. About how many times as stiff would it be if its thickness were tripled?
maths.explain: Tripling the thickness is 3 times 3 times 3. 3 times 3 is 9, and 9 times 3 is 27. So the plank would be about 27 times as stiff.
maths.why_maths: The stiffness of a plank grows with the cube of its thickness. A small change in thickness gives a big change in stiffness, and powers are the tool to see how big.

maths.problem: Five loose sheets of paper laid on each other are only 5 times as stiff as one sheet, because they slide. Five sheets glued into one act like a sheet 5 times as thick, so they are 5 times 5 times 5 times as stiff. How many times stiffer is the glued stack than the loose stack?
maths.explain: The glued stack is 5 times 5 times 5, which is 125 times as stiff as one sheet. The loose stack is 5 times as stiff. 125 divided by 5 is 25. So the glued stack is 25 times stiffer than the loose stack.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying and dividing show why gluing layers into one block is so much better than just stacking them.

maths.problem: A strip of cloth cut along the threads stretched 0.2 centimetres out of a 20 centimetre length. A strip cut on the slant stretched 4 centimetres out of 20 centimetres. What percentage of its length did each strip stretch? How many times more did the slant strip stretch?
maths.answer: 1 percent and 20 percent. The slant strip stretched 20 times more.
maths.explain: 0.2 out of 20 is 1 out of 100, which is 1 percent. 4 out of 20 is 1 out of 5, which is 20 percent. 20 divided by 1 is 20. So the slant strip stretched 20 times more.
maths.context: In the Tailor's Trick test, you hang a bottle from a cloth strip cut along the threads and one cut on the slant, and measure how much each stretches.
maths.why_maths: A percentage shows the stretch as a share of the original length, so strips of different lengths can be compared fairly.

maths.problem: A fatigue machine bends a wire 500 times each minute. How many hours and minutes will it take to reach 100,000 bends?
maths.explain: 100,000 divided by 500 is 200 minutes. 200 minutes is 3 hours and 20 minutes, because 3 hours is 180 minutes and 20 minutes are left over.
maths.why_maths: Engineers count bends in thousands and millions. Dividing the total by the rate turns a huge number of bends into a time you can picture.

maths.problem: Plywood boards are made with an odd number of layers. A maker has stacks of 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8 layers. Which stacks can she use? If each layer is 2 millimetres thick, how thick is the 7-layer board?
maths.answer: The stacks of 3, 5 and 7 layers. The 7-layer board is 14 millimetres thick.
maths.explain: A number is odd if it cannot be split into two equal groups. So 3, 5 and 7 are odd. 7 layers of 2 millimetres is 7 times 2, which is 14 millimetres.
maths.why_maths: An odd number of layers puts the same grain direction on both faces, so the board is balanced and stays flat. Odd and even numbers decide the design.

maths.problem: In the paper bridge test, the flat sheet carried 2 coins. The zigzag bridge carried 34 coins. How many times as many coins did the zigzag carry? The tube carried 51 coins. How many more coins did the tube carry than the zigzag?
maths.answer: 17 times as many. The tube carried 17 more.
maths.explain: 34 divided by 2 is 17. So the zigzag carried 17 times as many coins. 51 take away 34 is 17. So the tube carried 17 more coins than the zigzag.
maths.context: In the Paper Bridges activity, you load four paper bridges with coins to see which shape carries the most.
maths.why_maths: Comparing results by how many times as much shows how big the effect of shape was. Taking away shows the size of the gap between two designs.

maths.problem: Three clips snapped after 8, 10 and 9 big bends. Three more snapped after 26, 31 and 27 small bends. Find the average for each group. About how many times more small bends than big bends did it take?
maths.answer: 9 big bends and 28 small bends. About 3 times as many.
maths.explain: 8 plus 10 plus 9 is 27, and 27 divided by 3 is 9. 26 plus 31 plus 27 is 84, and 84 divided by 3 is 28. 28 divided by 9 is a little more than 3. So small bends took about 3 times as many.
maths.context: In the Bend Until It Snaps test, you bend paper clips by big bends and by small bends, and count how many bends each takes to snap.
maths.why_maths: An average smooths out the differences between single clips, so you can compare the two groups fairly.

maths.problem: A shelf plank is 2 centimetres thick and holds a load with a sag of 16 millimetres. You swap it for a plank of the same wood that is 4 centimetres thick. Using the rule that doubling the thickness makes a plank 8 times as stiff, what sag do you expect? Why can you not simply halve it?
maths.answer: About 2 millimetres. Halving would give 8 millimetres, but the stiffness grows eight times.
maths.explain: The thicker plank is about 8 times as stiff, so it sags about 8 times less. 16 divided by 8 is 2 millimetres. Halving would be right only if the stiffness doubled, but it grows by 2 times 2 times 2.
maths.why_maths: Predicting a result from a rule lets you check an idea before building anything, and compare the real result with the prediction.

roots.context: We have found that paper, wood, bamboo and cloth have a direction. Now we ask what that tells us about the things we call the same all the way through, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: A sheet of newspaper tears straight one way and crooked the other. The paper did not change. Its fibres lie mostly one way, so it has a direction built in. One number for how strong paper is leaves out which way you pull.
deep_truth.habit: We write one value for a material, such as 'paper is weak' or 'wood is strong', as if a property pointed nowhere. That hides the direction of the pull.
deep_truth.evidence: In the tear test, the same newspaper tore straight along its grain and crookedly across it. In the droop test, strips cut along the grain drooped less than strips cut across. Cloth cut on the slant stretched far more than cloth cut along its threads. If your own results differ, write them down as they are and test again.

three.who_am_i: Your bones are built of layers, and the struts inside them tend to line up with the way you stand and walk. Your body is built with directions in it.
three.what_is_life: A tree that is swayed by the wind grows a thicker trunk. A leaning tree makes special wood on one side to stand up again. A living body keeps a record of the pushes it has felt.
three.what_is_this_world: Paper still carries the direction of the belt it was made on, and wood carries the direction of the cells that the tree grew. Things carry their past inside them as a direction.

roots.thread: Zoom into a sheet of paper and you see thin fibres lying mostly one way. Zoom into wood and you see long tubes. Zoom into a metal and you see tiny crystals made of rows of atoms. At every size, a material is made of smaller parts placed in an arrangement. The direction comes from the arrangement. So what a material is depends on how its parts are placed, as well as on what they are.

teachings.teaching: People are born soft and bendy, and they die stiff and hard. Green plants are soft and full of sap, and they die dry and brittle. So the stiff and hard belong to death, and the soft and yielding belong to life. A tree that cannot bend is easily broken.
teachings.link: Bamboo bends a long way in a storm and springs back, because its fibres run unbroken. The brittle strips in our tests snapped.

teachings.teaching: Uddalaka teaches his son that when you know one lump of clay, you know everything made of clay. The pots and plates are only names, and the truth of each is clay.
teachings.link: A spoon, a tumbler and a bowl of steel are one material in different shapes. Our paper bridge showed that a shape changes how stiff a thing is, and the material stays the same.

teachings.teaching: A carpenter walks past a huge old oak and calls it useless, because its wood is twisted and cannot be sawn into planks. That night the oak speaks to the carpenter in a dream and says that this is why they have lived so long.
teachings.link: A carpenter reads the grain of wood before cutting. Twisted grain means a crooked plank, and the tree was left alone.

other_view.view: The direction is not a surprise or a flaw. A full description of a material's stiffness already includes every direction, in a table of numbers. A single number such as 'paper is strong' was only ever a shorthand, and nothing deeper is hidden in it.

how_we_found_out.story: In the 1800s, trains carried more and more people. The iron axles under the carriages sometimes snapped, even though they had been tested with loads far above what they carried. Many engineers thought the shaking changed the iron inside, turning it from long fibres into brittle crystals. The broken ends did look bright and grainy, which seemed to prove it. A German railway engineer named August Wöhler did not accept this. From the 1850s, he built machines that spun axles under a fixed load for millions of turns, and counted the turns until each one broke. He found that an axle lasted more turns when the load was smaller, and that below a certain load it might not break at all. The grainy look was simply what a fresh break looks like in iron. The iron had not changed. A small crack had grown a little with every turn. Counting the turns to failure is still how engineers test materials today.
how_we_found_out.who: August Wöhler, a German railway engineer (1819 to 1914)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Many engineers thought that shaking turned iron into brittle crystals. Wöhler showed that tiny cracks grow a little with each repeated load, and that a smaller load means more turns before the break.
